sections.h2: Columbia housing and who owns homes
sections.html:
Columbia is the seat of Boone County in central Missouri, about 120 miles from both St. Louis and Kansas City. Population was estimated at 130,851 on July 1, 2025. Fewer than half of homes are owner-occupied, at 48.7 percent, and with the university, three hospital systems and state government nearby, many houses in town have spent time as rentals.

The median owned home is worth $284,600, and median gross rent is $1,097. With 66.54 square miles of land in the city, value swings with the side of town and the distance to the university. Hinkson, Perche and Flat Branch creeks run through town, so check the flood map for any house near a stream valley.

Almost all of the city is in Columbia Public Schools, whose four high schools are Hickman, Rock Bridge, Muriel Battle and Frederick Douglass. A very small part of the city is in the Hallsville R-IV district.

Every rental unit in Columbia needs a Certificate of Compliance, and it is unlawful to operate a rental without a current one. A buyer of a former rental will want to know the certificate is valid.

A transferred certificate carries over for the unexpired part of its term. Applying involves an HVAC certification for gas appliances, then an inspection. Neighborhood Services at 11 N. Seventh Street, phone 573-817-5050, handles applications and transfers.

The city's Housing and Neighborhood Services department runs several programs that touch a house sale. Its Office of Neighborhood Services handles code enforcement at 573-817-5050, and the Housing Programs Division at 573-874-6321 runs federal and local housing aid.

  • The Homeownership Assistance Program helps make buying more affordable for eligible buyers.
  • The Home Rehab and Energy Efficiency Program brings existing homes up to property maintenance and rehabilitation standards.
  • The Neighborhood Cleanup Program supports block cleanups.

If you are selling to an owner-occupant, ask the Housing Programs Division whether the buyer's assistance program has any condition standards that your house would need to meet.

sections.h2: Boone County property taxes at a sale
sections.html:
The Boone County Collector mails tax statements in November, and real estate tax is due upon receipt but no later than December 31.

The tax stays attached to the property as a lien, so a new owner is liable for any unpaid amount. Buyer and seller usually prorate the year, and the buyer is credited at closing for the months the seller owned the house. No money is paid to the collector at the sale itself. A closing on or after October 1 can leave the bill in your name, so give the collector the new owner's name and address.

The assessor values a house at 19 percent of its market value for tax purposes. Delinquent parcels may go to a public tax certificate sale on the fourth Monday in August. Boone County also has a Senior Real Estate Tax Relief Program for approved primary residences.

sections.h2: Selling a former rental step by step
sections.html:
If the house has been leased, work through the city side before you talk price. First, find out whether the Certificate of Compliance is current, because operating without one is unlawful. Second, check how many years remain on the five-year term. A buyer who plans to keep renting will value a certificate with time left, and the transfer is cheap at $15 when it is filed within 90 days of title transfer.

Third, if the certificate has lapsed, plan on a new application, an HVAC certification for any gas appliances and an inspection. Fourth, tell the title company and the buyer what you found. A house that has a valid certificate and tidy records closes with fewer questions than one that needs the city's sign-off first.

Owners who would rather not do this work sometimes sell as is to a cash buyer. The buyer then deals with the certificate, but you should still share what you know and keep the paperwork.

Closing in Boone County follows a predictable order. The title company searches the record, checks that the year's tax is accounted for, and splits it with the buyer getting a credit for the months you owned the house. Nothing goes to the Collector from the closing table. Afterward, the deed is filed at the Government Center on East Walnut, and the Assessor updates the boundary maps from warranty deeds the recorder receives.

Bring photo identification, your payoff letter and the keys, and ask the title company which documents you need to sign in advance. Once closed, if the next bill could still reach you, tell the Collector who the new owner is and where to mail it.

Deeds for Columbia addresses are filed at the Boone County Government Center, 801 East Walnut, Room 132, in Columbia. The phone number is 573-886-4345. The office records real estate documents, including deeds, deeds of trust, releases and easements, and it is the source your title company will use for a clean history of the parcel.

Property boundary maps are updated by the Assessor's office from warranty deeds the recorder receives.

Older Columbia houses with tenants in place or a lapsed rental certificate can be harder to sell on the open market. Before you list, confirm the certificate status with Neighborhood Services, and if the house was a rental, ask what an inspection would look at. A gas appliance needs an HVAC certification before the inspection, so book that visit first and keep the certification paperwork for the file.

Buyers' inspectors in Columbia will also look hard at air conditioning, attic ventilation, roofs, gutters and older plumbing. Service the equipment and keep the receipts, because a seller who can show maintenance records usually gets fewer repair requests.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a Columbia house fast
sections.html:
In Columbia you can list with an agent, sell on your own, or accept an investor's as-is offer. Because tenants or a lapsed certificate make a listing harder, owners of those houses often look at a direct purchase.

Gather your payoff letter, Boone County tax statement, rental certificate status and school district first. That packet lets you compare a listing's net proceeds against a cash offer without delay. A cash sale skips the buyer's loan approval and appraisal. It still needs the tax split, the certificate transfer for a rental, and the recorded deed.

faqs.q: Does a Columbia rental certificate transfer to the buyer?
faqs.a: Yes. The city allows transfer within 90 days of title transfer for a $15 fee, and the certificate keeps its unexpired term. Call Neighborhood Services at 573-817-5050 to arrange it.

faqs.q: When are Boone County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Upon receipt of the bill, and no later than December 31. The Collector mails statements in November.

faqs.q: Who pays the property tax at closing?
faqs.a: Taxes are generally prorated, with the buyer credited by the seller for the months the seller owned the house. No tax money is paid to the collector's office at closing.

faqs.q: Where is the Boone County Recorder of Deeds?
faqs.a: At the Boone County Government Center, 801 East Walnut, Room 132 in Columbia. Call 573-886-4345 with questions about copies or filings.

faqs.q: Which school district serves my Columbia house?
faqs.a: Almost all of the city is in Columbia Public Schools, and a very small part lies in the Hallsville R-IV district. Check the district boundary for your address.
